title: Burn Claims Run 28% Higher in the Diwali Quarter, Star Health Data Shows
excerpt: The insurer's FY26 claims analysis shows the festive-quarter spike widening from 19% in FY25 — and sets out the six safety steps and the first aid that actually helps.
body:
• Burn-related insurance claims in the October-December quarter ran 28% above the average of the other three quarters in FY26, up from a 19% gap in FY25, Star Health's claims data shows.
  • The insurer says the same preventable patterns recur: crackers lit without adult supervision, duds relit or mishandled, and onlookers standing too close.
  • First aid that matters: cool a burn under running water for 10 to 20 minutes, and do not apply ice, toothpaste, oil, butter or turmeric.
  • Burns to the face, eyes, hands, feet or joints, or over a large area, need urgent medical care — do not burst blisters or pull off clothing stuck to the burn.

The Diwali quarter is measurably the burn season in India's insurance data. Star Health and Allied Insurance said burn-related claims reported in the third quarter (October-December) were 28% above the average of the other three quarters in FY26, compared with 19% in FY25, in a PR Newswire release sharing its claims analysis and safety guidance.

"Our claims data shows a clear pattern: in the Diwali quarter, burn-related claims run 28% above the average of the other three quarters. These injuries are largely preventable, and a few simple precautions can keep the celebration bright and joyful for everyone."

— Amitabh Jain, Chief Operating Officer, Star Health

How these injuries happen

Star Health says the patterns repeat every festive season: crackers lit without adult supervision, duds relit or mishandled, and onlookers standing too close. Ordinary causes fill out the list — sparks landing on synthetic clothing, loose garments drifting near a flame, or a hand reaching for a cracker that has not quite finished. The guidance aligns with the Directorate General of Health Services' firecracker safety guidelines.

The six steps, in full

The insurer's guide, also reported by SME Street, is: burst crackers only in open spaces, away from buildings, vehicles, wires and anything flammable, and never hold a cracker, anar, bomb or rocket in your hand while lighting it. Wear close-fitting cotton clothes and sturdy closed footwear, not loose or synthetic garments. Children should light crackers only as adults or under close adult supervision, and should be kept away from unexploded fireworks. Never relight a dud — douse it with water or sand before disposal.

If someone is burned

Cool the burned area under cool running water for 10 to 20 minutes. Do not apply ice, toothpaste, oil, butter, turmeric or other home remedies. Burns involving the face, eyes, hands, feet, joints or an extensive area require immediate medical care; do not burst blisters or remove clothing stuck to the burn. Star Health's point is timing: the first few minutes after an injury matter most, and prompt first aid plus timely medical attention can change how well a burn heals. For diaspora families celebrating Diwali in the US, the same first aid applies — cool running water first, then urgent care or emergency services for any burn in the categories above.

Star Health, which began operations in 2006 as India's first standalone health insurer, says it has settled over 1 crore claims, with a network of more than 17,000 hospitals and over 900 offices. Its Diwali release is a reminder aimed at its own policyholders as much as the public: burn injuries are among the most predictable festive-season claims it pays, and the quarter's 28% spike is the price, measured in its own book, of the same handful of mistakes repeated every year.
